title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
description: Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne matched a record-breaking donation anno
body: Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne matched a record-breaking donation announced late on Friday.Thailand-based Harborne wrote in the Telegraph, external that his "competitive spirit" inspired him to equal Ben Delo's donation - the largest ever given to a UK political party - adding he expected "nothing personally" in return.Reform said the £72m would be used to hire "the brightest and best minds to work on policy and the most comprehensive plan for government ever".The party is facing scrutiny over its finances, as the government seeks to cap donations to UK political parties from British expats.There have also been renewed calls by MPs from other political parties for donations from individuals to be capped.The £72m from the two donations is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year, which stood at just over £69m. Reform leader Nigel Farage said Harborne and Delo's "generosity" meant the party would "now be able to fight and win the next general election on a level playing field".A Reform UK spokesman added: "We will now also be able to hire up to 400 campaign managers in every target constituency. We are now on election footing."Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme on Saturday, the party's deputy leader Richard Tice denied accusations the donations were bad for democracy."It's the opposite actually, we're delighted and very humbled by the confidence expressed by two very successful entrepreneurs who realise Britain's in serious trouble," he said."To have that support, to know we can focus on employing the best people, whether it be on social media, policy, campaign managers, that's a good thing."Earlier, speaking to Sky News, Tice said Delo's donation had been an upfront sum "so that the Labour Party can't legislate against it" and would be spent over two or three years.Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations. The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage"."A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.However, the Labour government has introduced a £100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.There were nine donations of £1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was £9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.Labour had five donations of £1m or more - totalling nearly £10m - and the Conservatives had three of £1m each.Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of £500,000.She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding:  "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."Labour MP Stella Creasy and other backbenchers had proposed an amendment to the Government's Representation of the People Bill that would stop donors giving parties over £100,000 a year.But the amendment was never debated in the Commons after the government said it would set up a task force to investigate the issue. The bill will be debated in the House of Lords on Monday.Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging £72m to one political party in less than 48 hours."This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

schema.headline: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record

title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down
description: ByPaulin Kola and Lily JamaliNorth America Technology correspondentReporting fromSan FranciscoThe head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace
body: ByPaulin Kola and Lily JamaliNorth America Technology correspondentReporting fromSan FranciscoThe head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored.In an essay, Dario Amodei said developing AI was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious" and companies and governments must be given time to address them.The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei.There have been growing concerns recently about the technology's potential risks. An AI researcher who left Anthropic this week told the BBC that "if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future".Jacob Coxon told Laura Kuenssberg that people working at AI companies were "genuinely frightened... genuinely concerned about the fate of humanity in the next two years"."It's not at all an exaggeration to say that the people who are involved with both founding these companies and building the tech believe there is a possibility of human extinction," Coxon said."Many of the people who are sort of deep in the weeds on actually coding the thing believe that there is like a greater than ten percent chance, or even greater. Some smaller, but they all have different numbers for a probability that humans might die. And they all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology."In his essay, called We Must Pace the Frontier and made public on Saturday, Amodei proposed a three-point plan that includes independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation.As his proposal made the rounds, even competitors voiced support for the idea of third-party monitors who could evaluate the safety of models as they are developed."I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," wrote OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on X. He called independent evaluators "a great idea."In a new interview with Fortune Magazine, Altman had sounded similar safety concerns, saying standards were "not at a place" to push AI capabilities much further.He added that he believed AI beyond human control is "absolutely" possible.Elon Musk meanwhile said the Anthropic boss was "right". The warnings have prompted calls to action, but US President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".Some observers have also suggested that Amodei's post may be less about safety than about consolidating control over AI technology.Cyber-security concerns have grown as new models have exhibited more and more powerful hacking capabilities.Anthropic withheld its Mythos model from public use when it was announced in April that it could independently escape the testing environment, known as the sandbox.In the run-up to the release of its most recent Astra model, OpenAI cited cybersecurity concerns as it explained it had paused certain aspects of the model's development.Safety has also taken centrestage in the rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI.Amodei, who had previously worked as a vice president at OpenAI, has said he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 so he could build safer and more trusted AI models.In his essay, Amodei pointed out that AI had advanced "drastically faster" including its "ability to build the next generation of AI" - and mentioned an incident involving rival OpenAI which has revealed that agents conducted cybersecurity attacks, external on targets they were not asked to attack in July.The OpenAI agents had "essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective", Amodei said. OpenAI has said it is slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools as a result.Amodei called for "building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits".This would not mean "halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this". He was committing Anthropic to this "unilaterally" - as well as calling on governments "to require other frontier companies to match".Amodei said he recognised that regulation might not be able to keep up with the pace of AI, and therefore called on AI companies to "voluntarily work together to set standard" in parallel with regulation. The Anthropic CEO went on to address the impact that a slowdown would have on the industry and competition with leading developers worldwide, particularly China."I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei said. This would have to be done in a co-ordinated manner "without sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI". Any slowdown would have to be limited, he said, to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.He urged the US government to take measures so that US companies' AI chips could not be sold to China - or the technology shared with authoritarian countries.  His former employee, Jacob Coxon, told the BBC, however, that the initiative to slow down must go beyond the US - "there'll need to be some sort of co-ordinated slowdown with China if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".Amodei's post has prompted a wide range of responses.Clement Delangue, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, said he was launching a new project called the Open Alignment Initiative, adding he wanted to be among "embedded evaluators" that Amodei proposed could be part of a solution.Hugging Face was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety."Let's make AI safer by making it more transparent." Delangue wrote on X.Elon Musk also voiced his support, writing that "Dario is right".Musk, whose SpaceXAI makes the controversial chatbot Grok, once called Anthropic "evil" but has changed his tone since signing a $15bn deal to sell compute capacity to Anthropic in May.However some observers suggested that Amodei's post was less about safety than about consolidating control over AI technology."Dario makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic," wrote Chamath Palihapitiya, investor and co-host of the tech podcast "All-In".Notions of slowing down or even pausing AI development have long been met with such cynicism in certain corners of Silicon Valley, with critics accusing leading AI developers of hyping their technology as a marketing ploy.Anthropic and OpenAI are both reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings.

schema.headline: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down

title: I couldn't experience my baby scan, but blind parents like me can now feel them
description: When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the h
body: When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat.But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby.Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme.At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment.Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did".But he said the 20-week scan was more positive."The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says.They also now have the model of their 20-week scan picture, through the scheme by the charity Guide Dogs."I can't stop feeling it to be honest," Reece says."It's so nice to be able to fully access something without the need for other people's descriptions or interpretations. It has enough detail that I know what things are and it just makes everything feel more real."It's an innovation which has made me reflect on my own experiences of pregnancy and parenting.Before my partially sighted husband and I started trying for kids, I researched absolutely everything it would entail, from how to use specialist apps to read pregnancy test results, to the bells and squeaky shoes I could use to keep tabs on a fast-moving toddler.I immediately discovered a community of people in my position ready to share their wisdom, and a host of tried and tested workarounds for almost every scenario.But a decade on, there are even more advances, and I've spoken to other blind parents to find out the best ways they tackle the challenges they face.For Kim and Sean Randall, who have a teenager and an 11-month-old, the progress of technology is one of the biggest changes they have noticed in the 15 years between the births of their children.For their youngest child, maternity notes came in an app which could be accessed with a screen reader on their phone, rather than being handwritten in the traditional NHS blue book.Kim says it put her on more of an equal footing with other expectant parents, and helped her feel more in control."I could check the notes, and any test results, when I wanted rather than waiting to have them read to me," she says.For the 20-week scan, she says Sean had researched the meaning of the different numbers on an ultrasound - like the baby's thigh length or head circumference - and used a specialist AI screen-reading app to have the text read out and the images described.Some parents say they prefer this method to a 3D model, because they can get more detail from audio description of the image than from physical touch.But it's not just scans where visually impaired parents can struggle.Reece, like many blind parents, says he wants to be extra prepared for when the baby comes, "so I don't get in the way or feel like a liability"."We've been labelling clothes, putting Braille in baby books and organising the baby bag so that I know where everything is," he says.Kim, meanwhile, runs Facebook and WhatsApp groups for blind mums. Together, we have collated a host of tips and tricks from blind parents over the years for what to do when the baby arrives.They include things like:Carry your own folding mat for nappy changes and always have everything you need close at handWhen changing a nappy, if you think you can stop, "keep wiping" - and use barrier cream, because the start of a nappy rash can be hard to feelScore a raised mark on any syringes or scoops you might use for making up feeds so you know where to fill them toUse a baby carrier or pram which can be pulled as well as pushed, in case you walk with a guide dog or cane in front of you to get aroundOnce they start toddling, bells clipped to clothing are a handy way of knowing where they are at homeWhen weaning, use a wipeable high chair with a waterproof mat underneath, to keep mess contained and know what they've eaten and what's gone on the floorThe Royal National Institute of Blind People , external(RNIB) has also produced guides for expectant parents and those with young children.They suggest ideas like using baby gates to block off the kitchen when you are removing something from the oven, or the hall when you are answering the door.For parents who have some but not total visual impairment, Kim says children can be dressed in brightly coloured clothing while out and about so they are easier to spot."I put them in feelable clothes so I don't grab the wrong child," says Kim, who has no vision."One of my favourites is a shirt with a castle on it. You open the door and there's a dragon inside."When her eldest started walking, she says "we always held hands, but had a wrist strap connecting us in case she tried to run off".For me, clothes pegs were always useful for keeping outfits together wherever possible.Also consider buying socks the same style and colour - matching those is still a nightmare for me a decade later. If two items feel the same but are different colours, cut the label on one of them.

schema.headline: I couldn't experience my baby scan, but blind parents like me can now feel them

title: Insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
description: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hoste
body: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity. They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post."We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology."It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said."Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".  And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a monopoly in the sector.Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole".On Friday, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety."Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's  proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety. Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei.Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development."There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could.""When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added.If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China.Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now."But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal.David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic. OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership".OpenAI, which announced in June that it would go public on the stock market, was most recently valued at $852bn.The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment.At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI.One investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares.His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable?When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - CEO of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words."No," he said.

schema.headline: Insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley

title: World Athletics Ultimate Championship: Keely Hodgkinson second to Audrey Werro despite recent hamstring tear
description: Keely Hodgkinson was again denied a major prize by rival Audrey Werro - but revealed she had overcome a torn hamstring to make the start line at the W
body: Keely Hodgkinson was again denied a major prize by rival Audrey Werro - but revealed she had overcome a torn hamstring to make the start line at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship.Britain's Olympic 800m champion sustained the injury while competing in the European Championship final less than a month ago, when she was dethroned by 22-year-old Swiss sensation Werro.Hodgkinson was forced to miss Diamond League races in Zurich and Brussels, and said following her second-place finish in Budapest that it was "touch and go" whether she would be fit to compete at the sport's new global event.Werro controlled Saturday's 800m race from start to finish, winning in one minute 55.88 seconds to underline her position as the event's current leading athlete.Despite her injury setback, Hodgkinson overtook Femke Broeders-Bol on the home straight for second in 1:56.26."On the outside, people might think I'm disappointed - but I'm actually quite proud of how I approached that," Hodgkinson told BBC Sport."When was Europeans? Four weeks ago. I unfortunately tore my hamstring during that race, so I didn't know if I was going to be here. "It's been a bit of a frustrating season but, I think overall, I'm finishing second in the world and I can't really be too hard on myself for that."Each time the leading women's 800m trio have met this season, it has been billed as one of the races of the year. Each time, it has delivered enthralling action.Since beginning 2026 with a dominant indoor season in which she won world indoor gold and broke the indoor 800m world record, Hodgkinson has been second-best in meetings with Werro.Making remarkable progress in her first season as a full-time athlete, Werro continues to uncover what, increasingly, appears to be potential of history-making proportions since completing her university studies.Forty-three years had passed since a woman had run a sub-1:54 800m before this season. Werro achieved that three times this summer to close in on Jarmila Kratochvilova's 1983 record of 1:53.28.Although not required to go as fast on this occasion, she showed her maturity by controlling the final before surging to victory.Hodgkinson will be pleased to have still had enough to overhaul two-time world 400m hurdles champion Broeders-Bol, who has made rapid progress in her first season since switching events.On her burgeoning rivalry with Werro and Broeders-Bol, Hodgkinson said: "I honestly love it. I think it's really great for our sport and for women's sport to have so many amazing women pushing each other."I'm happy to be part of it. Hopefully, next time, I'll come out on top."I'm always there fighting. That's something to be proud of and take into the future. I'm only 24 and hopefully I'll be around for a lot longer."Although she missed out on the title, Hodgkinson, who will end her season at Athlos next weekend, pocketed $75,000 (£55,000) for her efforts.Athletes are competing for the biggest prize pot in the sport's history at the Ultimat Championship, with a total of $10m (£7.4m) on offer across three days of action.It is hoped that the condensed, innovative format, introduced to bring together the world's best athletes at the end of a season which otherwise would have lacked a global championship, can help shape the sport's future.Vivaldi, Reiki and sauna sessions with training partner Hodgkinson. That is how Georgia Hunter Bell reset to go agonisingly close to her fourth major title of a sensational season.The 32-year-old's remarkable return to the sport she had given up until late 2022 continued with European, Commonwealth and world indoor gold medals this year.But a busy season for Hunter Bell - this was the Olympic bronze medallist's 20th race - appeared to catch up with her at last week's Diamond League final, where she faded to fourth.After finishing runner-up to Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska by 0.17 seconds in a brilliant head-to-head down the home straight in Hungary, Hunter Bell - who clocked 3:57.72 - told BBC Sport: "I'm so proud of myself. I've done absolutely everything I could this year."I had to get myself into a stronger place mentally after last week. I didn't have the buzz that I usually do walking out."I listened to a lot of Vivaldi's Spring, a very hopeful song. I did Reiki to try and get rid of any bad energy. "I went to the spa with Keely - she made me sit in the sauna for like 20 minutes and sweat out all the bad energy. And I worked with my coaches to get my belief and hunger back. It was definitely there today on the home straight." In Saturday's penultimate race, Amy Hunt was disappointed by her eighth-place finish in a stacked women's 100m final, won by American world champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden ahead of Olympic gold medallist Julien Alfred.After winning her first individual global medal with 200m silver last year, the 24-year-old achieved a historic four gold medals at last month's Europeans.The next challenge, and ultimately Hunt's ambition, is to replicate that on the global stage - but she was unable to get close to Jefferson-Wooden, who triumphed in a world-leading 10.62 seconds, the joint-seventh fastest time in history.Hunt, who will return for the 200m on Sunday, told BBC Sport: "I feel a bit disassociated right now. That's the first time dealing with having a 100m semi, then having to regroup and go back out [for the final]."I don't think that I did myself very proud in that race but I'm lucky to be able to go to sleep tonight and come back out tomorrow in my more favourite event and see what happens."European champion Matthew Hudson-Smith faded to fifth in 44.28 seconds in the men's 400m final, as Botswana's Collen Kebinatshipi's ran the joint-fifth fastest time in history in 43.39.

schema.headline: World Athletics Ultimate Championship: Keely Hodgkinson second to Audrey Werro despite recent hamstring tear

title: Chess: 'I was beating adults at chess when I was eight'
description: Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan plays for Strand Chess Club in east BelfastByGráinne ConnollyBBC News NI"When I was eight or nine I wa
body: Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan plays for Strand Chess Club in east BelfastByGráinne ConnollyBBC News NI"When I was eight or nine I was beating adults at chess and they were raging when they lost, like 'I just lost to a little kid'."Ethan first became interested in chess when he was six years old after he spotted someone else playing.Now 13, he plays for Strand Chess Club in east Belfast and has represented Ireland through all his age groups.Last week he became the youngest Ulster chess champion in history – not just in his age category but across all ages."I was really surprised because I've never won any of the big tournaments before, I've always got so close and I managed to win it in the end," Ethan told BBC News NI.He said his opponents ranged from the ages of 30-65, all at least more than twice his age."That age range is the ages I've been playing against and I didn't get any losses. I got three wins and three draws."Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan has represented Ireland in his age groupsEthan said he enjoys the mental challenge of chess."I quite like the thinking part and the opening preparation."The game itself looks really interesting but there is so much more that goes into it before with preparation and tactics."I think I just had a natural ability from the start which I think was quite useful but I think starting at a young age helps quite a lot because it's easier to get it into your brain."I practice a lot and... I'm good at maths. I've got quite a good calculating ability. I think that's probably my main strength."'If you're good enough you're old enough'Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan and his mum Eimear who says his success is all down to himselfNeither of Ethan's parents are chess players.However, his mum Eimear Savage said her son was fascinated with the chess board and pieces the moment he first saw them."It was a chance circumstance that Ethan saw someone play chess and thought it looked interesting and he decided he wanted to play and it went from there." She said Ethan's success is all down to himself but his family support him every step of the way."I think Ethan just takes it in his stride and that's him. He enjoys playing chess and he enjoys taking part and when he wins it's a bonus."Ethan has been playing for a while now so people are used to playing against him but maybe when he was younger, I remember he wasn't quite tall enough to see over the table and he had to kneel up on the chair to get a good view of the pieces."That was always a bit of a spectacle but people know him now."Ethan has played as part of the Irish team and has travelled to Paris where he played at the Eiffel Tower, as well as travelling to the Netherlands, Germany and Estonia for tournaments.Tough opponentImage source, family handoutImage caption, Ethan has been beating adult opponents for many years on his way to becoming Ulster championEthan is certainly making a name for himself and his success isn't any surprise to his fellow members at Strand Chess Club.Gareth Annesley said Ethan is a very tough opponent."You wouldn't think he's that young. You think you've got him and he just keeps on playing these moves and it's hard to beat him. He's very resourceful and he's very mature for his age."Even though he's only 13 he's been around for several years, so he has more or less beaten most of the top players in Ulster, so it wasn't a complete shock."If you're good enough, you're old enough in chess really."So what's next for Ethan?"I'm going to keep this up for the rest of my life."My next goal is probably to be Irish champion and then grand master probably. That's the main goal."

schema.headline: Chess: 'I was beating adults at chess when I was eight'

title: Tottenham 0-0 Everton: Spurs blanked again as new era turns into a false dawn
description: The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help."Please Score A Goal" was t
body: The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help."Please Score A Goal" was the message brandished in the direction of the Spurs players as they came out against Everton in search of their first in the Premier League this season.After another goalless 45 minutes, there was a compelling case for a hasty rewrite asking "Please Have A Shot" as, for all their possession, Roberto de Zerbi's expensively assembled side struggled to get anywhere near Jordan Pickford's goal.And so it went on in an increasingly angry and frustrated atmosphere inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as Spurs' goalless league streak extended to 407 minutes as a stuttering start to what was meant to be brave new era continued.It was the first time they have failed to score in their opening four league games across all four tiers - and also in four successive Premier League matches since September 2006.The grim statistic would be bad enough in any circumstances, but it is even worse after Spurs spent in excess of £300m in the summer, much of it designed to give De Zerbi's side an added edge.Instead, they are a blunt instrument.This was the first Premier League goalless draw, in the 140th game, at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. On this evidence, there will be more.It may seem early days for an apology to the supporters, but De Zerbi felt the need as he said: "I'm sorry to the fans. We are sorry to the fans."They were fantastic, especially in the first part of the game because when they see the team is playing well, pushing to find the solution they were inside the pitch with my players. Then the reaction of the fans is normal. We have to say thanks all the time to them."Everton could have actually made matters worse, but they are also short of attacking threat themselves - luckily for Spurs.As the second half wore on, the resilient visitors actually missed the game's two best chances through Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Brennan Johnson, while the mood became increasingly sour as nerves and anxiety grew.When £85m summer signing Mateus Fernandes had Spurs' first shot on target after 46 minutes, the stadium rattled to the sound of ironic applause.There was no irony when they played the ball around at the back with only seven minutes left, and when the final whistle sounded it was just like old times - or at least like last season - as jeers sent De Zerbi's players on their way.He went through the card in an attempt to change this embarrassing barren sequence in front of goal, playing new signings from Manchester City, Omar Marmoush and Savio, in the attacking positions, with Dominic Solanke handed his first league start of the campaign.As time went on and the tension mounted, Mohammed Kudus and James Maddison were sent on, but it was another substitute, Lucas Bergvall, who almost snatched victory with a late long-range effort, saved by Everton goalkeeper Pickford after he had gifted the Swede possession and an opportunity.Watching it all from close quarters was a grim-faced Richarlison, the 29-year-old Brazil striker in dispute with the club over the remaining nine months of his contract.He was left out of De Zerbi's Premier League squad after a proposed deadline-day return to former club Everton collapsed. A switch back to Brazil with Vasco da Gama has also failed to materialise.The 'xG' - expected goals - statistic suggests Spurs should have scored three or four goals this season, but their non-penalty xG per shot this season is just 0.066. It gives them an expected conversion rate of 6.6%.In layman's terms, it means they are not very good when comes to creating an attacking threat.De Zerbi, never someone to disguise his emotions, grew more animated and irritated as the game went on, marching on to the pitch at the final whistle for an exchange with substitute Mathys Tel.When any side embarks on the sort of root and branch revolution the Italian presided over this summer, it is inevitable there will be teething problems and time required for understandings and relationships to form.And the change is understandable after two successive 17th-placed finishes in the Premier League. Indeed, Spurs' last league goal actually came against Everton on the final day of last season, courtesy of Joao Palhinha.It kept them in the top flight, allowing them to make a fresh start for this campaign.De Zerbi, who still has much work to do to rid Spurs of the aftershock of two poor seasons, said: "I think in the first 30 minutes we were very, good but we didn't find a goal. I think in that moment we suffer too much with confidence and this is another important part for us at the moment."In the second half, I observed many players had a little less confidence and I don't like this. They have to be happy and understand we are in the right way."The players are human and they have emotions and they think with their head. My position is to help them and stay focus on the improvement we have to do. If we play 90 minutes like we did in the first 30 minutes, I think we are going to win many games."Spurs, however, have a toothlessness that must be a concern. It is certainly one for the supporters who watched their players either take too long over chances or, on many occasions, passed on the responsibility.They also ran into a rugged Everton defence, with Jarrad Branthwaite magnificent as he stepped up his claims for a place in Thomas Tuchel's next England squad after injury troubles.For Spurs, however, there were few positives as the wait for a first Premier League win - and goal - this season goes on.

title: World's tallest living horse based in Towcester 'still growing'
description: 'He's massive!' Meet Hugo, the world's tallest horseImage source, GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS 2027Image caption, One of Hugo's owners, Lisa Masters, said h
body: 'He's massive!' Meet Hugo, the world's tallest horseImage source, GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS 2027Image caption, One of Hugo's owners, Lisa Masters, said he was "a big softie, like an oversized dog"ByAlex PopeA Shire horse that has entered the record books as the world's tallest living horse could exceed his height as he is still growing, his owner has said. Hugo, who lives in Towcester, Northamptonshire, has already reached an "abnormal" 199cm tall, about 6.5ft, or 19.2 hands, to the withers or ridge at the base of the neck.Guinness World Records said the four-year-old's stature was officially assessed by a vet and he was measured without shoes to ensure an accurate result.Owner Brett Masters said Hugo received "a huge amount of care" from a chiropractor, dentist, vet and masseuse, meaning he lived a "five-star lifestyle".Shire horses are known for their height and their large stature means they are able to pull heavy weight, which is why they have been historically used as working horses on farms and for transport.The tallest and heaviest horse ever documented, external was a Shire gelding named Sampson, who was later renamed Mammoth - bred by Thomas Cleaver of Toddington Mills in Bedfordshire, which stood at 2.19 metres - or 7ft 2.5 in - in 1850.Image source, Tove Valley Shire HorsesImage caption, Hugo has his teeth checked twice a year by his dentist, HannahMasters, from Tove Valley Shire Horses, said the breed was his passion. He was approached by officials from Guinness World Records as Hugo was "locally famous", and they had been told: "There is this really big horse, you need to speak to these guys."Masters said that when he acquired Hugo - at the age of 18 months - he had no idea he was "very tall, abnormally tall"."He's still got three years of growing left, he won't stop until he's about eight and a half, he's only a baby," he said."It will cause issues, so we have to be very careful with him."He has a chiropractor, has regular massages, the dentist visits every six months, and the vet checks him all the time as his growing plates are hyperactive. "He has lots of supplements and a careful feed regime."He lives a five-star lifestyle, he wants for nothing."Image source, GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS 2027Image caption, Brett Masters said when Hugo goes out and about, people stop to admire himMasters added: "Every time he goes out, people stop, they film him, shout at you that 'he's massive'."He's the kindest, most gentle kind of horse."He said he did not receive any form of payment for his official recognition, but joked: "If any carrot farmer wants to give him some carrots, he'd kindly have them." Hugo is kept busy by taking part in demonstrations and showing people what shire horses would have done "back in the day, by pulling agricultural implements, driving wagons", and is now learning to have people ride him. "He's very happy, and he just loves a good fuss," Masters added. Image source, Tove Valley Shire HorsesImage caption, Hugo is much taller than his half-brother, Masters saidDo you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

title: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
description: A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group ha
body: A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group has said.Princes - which supplies major supermarkets - has substituted jack mackerel, an entirely different species, for mackerel, with similar tins also being sold by Lidl.The switch has been spurred by dwindling stocks of Atlantic mackerel after years of overfishing, with its Chilean counterpart more sustainable and a third of the cost."It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional quality," Sue Davies, head of food policy at Which?, said.Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and around a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.The shift has prompted complaints from some consumers over differences in taste and texture, as well as concerns about how clearly the replacement fish is being labelled.Princes announced last October, external that it was changing all of its tinned mackerel products to jack mackerel, saying the species meets the Marine Stewardship Council's sustainability standards.The firm said its jack mackerel products were "clearly identified" and had been introduced following extensive product and consumer testing, describing it as having a "milder flavour and meatier texture".Lidl is selling jack mackerel under its house brand. Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries". Davies from Which? said: "While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe."She added: "Skimpflation - quietly changing ingredients to cut costs - has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."Despite its name, jack mackerel is not a type of mackerel. Jack mackerel belongs to the Carangidae fish family, while traditional mackerel belongs to the Scombridae family. Until December 2025, under UK law, Carangidae species could only be marketed as "jack", "scad", "trevally" or "horse mackerel".But shortly after Princes launched its new product as "jack mackerel", the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs changed its rules to permit the labelling.Industry figures reposted by seafood market intelligence platform Undercurrent suggest wholesale Chilean jack mackerel costs roughly one-third as much as  Atlantic mackerel.The Scottish Pelagic Fishermen's Association said there was the potential for confusion, saying "consumers should be able to clearly understand what they are buying".CEO designate Hannah Fennell said: "If retailers move away from Northeast Atlantic mackerel, they are unfairly punishing the UK industry while instead sourcing a different, less omega-3-rich species from the other side of the world with a significantly higher carbon footprint to the UK market."The switch follows the so-called "mackerel war", a long-running dispute between the UK, Iceland, Greenland, Norway, the Faroe Islands, the EU and Russia over shared mackerel catch quotas.The countries have repeatedly failed to agree a unified system for sharing stock and setting catch limits in line with scientific advice.Mackerel catches in the north-east Atlantic have exceeded the levels advised by scientists by an average of 39% over the past 15 years, according to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC). Stocks have plummeted by roughly three-quarters over the past decade, according to the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (Ices).The intergovernmental body has advised slashing the quantity of north-east Atlantic mackerel caught in 2026 by roughly 70% to allow the stock a chance to recover.Last year, the Marine Conservation Society said the Atlantic mackerel population was at "breaking point".The severe depletion of mackerel numbers has led to the fish losing its MSC certification, meaning it no longer complies with many retailers' sustainability policies. Chilean jack mackerel, in contrast, is MSC-certified.In February, Waitrose said it would suspend sales of fresh, chilled and frozen mackerel due to overfishing concerns, while tinned products would be phased out as existing stock was sold.The Marine Conservation Society heralded the move as "leading and decisive".The switch to jack mackerel is being felt beyond the UK, with supermarkets in the Netherlands no longer selling Atlantic mackerel and at least one supermarket in Sweden switching to jack mackerel.

schema.headline: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves

title: Teen boy rescued after days adrift in Alaskan waters
description: That vessel was also able to recover the bodies of his two relatives."Our hearts go out to the families, friends, and communities affected by the trag
body: That vessel was also able to recover the bodies of his two relatives."Our hearts go out to the families, friends, and communities affected by the tragic loss of these two mariners," said Rear Adm. Bob Little, the commander of the Coast Guard's Arctic District.The boy had signs of hypothermia when he was rescued, the USCG said.The captain of the fishing boat that pulled Aghnaanga to safety told a local Anchorage news outlet that the teen had clung to the skiff through darkness and water temperatures around 50F (10C)."That's one tough kid," the captain, Adam White, told KTUU-TV."Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff," White added. "And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away."Their fishing boat capsized on Saturday, leaving Aghnaanga without food or water for two days at sea, the boy's mother wrote on Facebook.Vina Kulowiyi, the mother of Aghnaanga and his older brother, said her sons were doing what they loved: fishing to provide for members of their community who don't always have access to meat at their local store in Savoonga. Savoonga - a village of around 800 residents, located on St Lawrence Island off Alaska's coast - is primarily inhabited by Siberian Yupik peoples. English and St Lawrence Island Yupik are the island's main languages. "My boys were born and raised to be providers. A tradition that is passed on," Kulowiyi wrote on Facebook. "We hunt and provide for families and share the community."Kulowiyi said her surviving son is recovering at home. "My survivor," she wrote. "His story is amazing. He was never afraid the whole time." He sat "praying the whole time", she added.

title: Bulgaria investigates fire at weapons  site that owner calls sabotage
description: Bulgaria is investigating the cause of an overnight fire at an ammunition storage site run by a private defence company.Interior Minister Ivan Demerdz
body: Bulgaria is investigating the cause of an overnight fire at an ammunition storage site run by a private defence company.Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the authorities "are not ruling out outside interference" in the incident in central Bulgaria. No-one was injured in the blaze that triggered a series of explosions.EMCO company, whose weapons are used by Ukraine against invading Russian forces, said the fire at its site was sabotage and that human error was "completely ruled out". It did not say who might be responsible.The latest incident follows last month's fire and blasts at another EMCO ammunition warehouse in the area. In a statement, EMCO said the storage facility that was burned this time - near the central village of Gorni Varpishta, some 170km (106 miles) east of the capital Sofia -   had not been used for months and was inspected just 20 days ago, when full compliance with all regulations was confirmed.It cited a number of similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, saying that the latest was "no exception to the series of acts of sabotage against the Bulgarian defence industry"."As the EU and Nato member state most severely affected by such actions, Bulgaria must join the collective effort to prevent and neutralise these attacks," EMCO said.The firm is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors allege has already been targeted by Russian agents.This includes a poisoning attempt in 2015 of Gebrev, his son and another company employee - three Russian nationals were later charged in absentia for attempted murder.Bulgaria is a major weapons supplier to Ukraine, as it continues to repel a full-scale Russian invasion launched in 2022.And although Sofia has recently halted state-owned arms supplies to Ukraine, Bulgarian private defence companies continue such transfers.Russia appears to have recently escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd".There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

schema.headline: Bulgaria investigates fire at weapons  site that owner calls sabotage

title: Trump: US president's comments on a united Ireland may have targeted an audience across the Atlantic
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, US President Donald Trump is visiting IrelandByCaitriona PerryChief PresenterReporting fromin DublinWhen another w
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, US President Donald Trump is visiting IrelandByCaitriona PerryChief PresenterReporting fromin DublinWhen another world leader meets US President Donald Trump the only certainty about what might happen is the uncertainty about what might happen. This was exactly the case ahead of President Trump's two-day visit to Ireland. Nobody could have predicted that by the end of the first day, the main global headline would be his desire to see a unified Ireland.As the shockwaves of his remarks rippled through this island and Great Britain, it was unclear whether this represented a new US administration policy, or an off-the-cuff remark from a president who likes to take questions from reporters, and likes to give answers.Image source, ReutersImage caption, President Trump with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál MartinFormer Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney was Trump's special envoy to Northern Ireland in his first term in office. He cautioned against anyone reading too much into the president's remarks. "This does not represent a shift in US  foreign policy," he said."We're still very much committed to the Good Friday Agreement."Democratic Congressman Brendan Boyle agreed."There is bipartisan support for that deal, and that is not going to change."Although both agreed that Donald Trump was probably right to say that "eventually" unification would happen, that did not mean the US was about to start pushing for it.Figure caption, Watch: President Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unifiedGiving an answer to a question that is asked at a free-flowing press conference is one thing, but Donald Trump repeated his sentiments a short time later when he was delivering a speech to an invited audience at the US Ambassador's residence. In fact it was almost the first thing he mentioned, hinting that maybe he realised he had kicked over a can of worms at his earlier appearance.The rest of that speech was curious. It was billed as a 20-minute address to Irish and Irish American business leaders, but was about twice that and strayed largely into domestic US matters.President Trump has a speaking style that he describes himself as "the weave". He can bounce from topic to topic during any speaking engagement, veering off the script and then returning to the matter at hand. Today he lauded his own achievements, as he sees them, such as clamping down on illegal immigration, doing deals and boosting defence production. He repeated his criticisms once again of what he views as the UK's lack of support for his military operation in Iran.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Donald Trump meets Irish President Catherine ConnollyMidterm elections fast approachingBut who was his target audience? The gathered business leaders in Dublin or a US audience tuning in before it was even dawn in much of that country?  This November's crunch midterm elections are fast approaching and the Republican party is under intense pressure because of the president's policies. They may lose control of one or both houses of Congress.About one tenth of the US population claim Irish heritage but they are not a homogeneous voting bloc. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Clinton alongside former Irish President Mary Robinson in 1995Was he trying to target Irish-American independent or swing voters in the US, of which there are many who have flip-flopped between the Republican and Democratic party in recent years? Some of them do support a unified Ireland and so in this time of chasing every vote, perhaps that played a part.Bill Clinton secured a lot of Irish-American support when he was running for president, by promising to get engaged in the peace process. They voted for him and he followed through on his promise and much of that work led to the foundations of the Good Friday Agreement. But, Irish America is a different place now. Indeed, America is a different place now as politics have become more polarised. The November election campaigns show no indication that will change anytime soon. But political leaders in Ireland will be hoping the only debate tomorrow is about the play on the golf course.

schema.headline: Trump: US president's comments on a united Ireland may have targeted an audience across the Atlantic

title: Anti-migrant activists like Danny Tommo are changing tactics
description: At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston
body: At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham. The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground. In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL)."I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth. His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France. On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings. "These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said."This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.Its organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.The website for Patriot Platform was registered on 18 May this year, two days after a big anti-immigration "Unite the Kingdom" march in London.Thomas, its most visible founder, first posted about the group on YouTube on 8 June."We need to be a bit smarter," he said, referencing arrests or offences including the assaults on police officers and violent disorder during recent Unite the Kingdom marches, that had been organised by Robinson. "Good men and women are now away from the fight stuck in jail cells." Thomas told his supporters he had a few ideas that would be "more powerful than committing acts of violence and criminal damage".There needs to be a "different MO", he said. "We are looking for the strong, the able, the ones that are willing to do things a bit different."What sets Patriot Platform apart is the scale and co-ordination of their action, says William Allchorn of Anglia Ruskin University, an expert on far-right movements. "There hasn't [previously] been co-ordinated mass activism with hundreds of people descending and trying to take matters, as it were, into their own hands," he says.Thomas spent the summer posting further videos about the group and staging meetings in the North West, Essex, Leicester and Kent. He said he was trying to organise a "mass resistance" movement.What happened in Dover demonstrated some of his new ways of working. The protesters were almost exclusively male. They arrived in well-organised waves in the backs of lorries. They did not engage with the media, and said little to members of the public whose journeys and weekends they were disrupting.Then, after a few hours, before the police could get organised, the men all marched off to Dover Priory Station and left. Estimates vary as to how many were there but it looks like between 200 and 500.The anti-racism group Hope Not Hate said Patriot Platform should be seen "for what it is: a far-right network of men happy to intimidate and inconvenience an entire town for what was effectively a publicity stunt".Nick Lowles, the group's CEO, said Thomas had "been upfront about his intention to create a 'patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom'".At a protest outside the Daily Mail offices in London on Wednesday, Thomas could be seen giving clear instructions to his supporters about his preferred tactics."Don't intimidate anyone," he ordered. "No one talk. Keep a distance. Five metres away from police".Patriot Platform is coming into a crowded space of activists campaigning against immigration. Robinson's is the most high-profile brand. A former close associate of Danny Thomas, Robinson (whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon) has given Patriot Platform public support since Saturday. But there is also Paul Golding's Britain First, Turning Point UK and the neo-Nazi Patriotic Alternative.Thomas was once close to Ryan Bridge, the founder of a group called Raise the Colours, who have put up flags in towns across England over the last year. But the pair have since publicly fallen out, with Thomas telling Bridge in an online rant: "Do I need to stab you in the eye?"Thomas was jailed for two years in 2016 after he and two others tried to kidnap a man at knifepoint in Portsmouth in a dispute over money linked to drugs. What seems to be different about Patriot Platform's approach now is that Thomas is explicitly talking about creating a "voting bloc" of supporters to back a yet-to-be decided party, which offers policies closest to what he wants, at the next general election."I do not support any political party at this moment in time," he said, adding that once the bloc was established, it would be made "extremely clear" which way the group's vote would go. It's not clear whether Reform UK would get his backing. In a public confrontation with Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth on Monday, Thomas complained that Nigel Farage had branded his Dover protest "disgusting"."The working class do not vote," Thomas said. "We are going to make it a fashionable thing to take all your family members to the voting booth."But if your leader keeps slandering people, it's going to push them to other parties."Waiting in the wings is the new party Restore Britain, launched by Rupert Lowe after he was suspended from Reform UK. On X, the party said it "stands with the patriots peacefully protesting against the invasion".  It is not clear how much support Thomas has. Parties like Reform and Restore will be very aware of the potential power that activists like Thomas and Robinson can now wield with their large social media followings. On X, Robinson has two million followers to Farage's 2.3 million, while Thomas has almost 163,000.At Wednesday's protest, Thomas offered to pay supporters for any work they had missed to be there - in cash.This kind of generosity might help explain why his activism - and that of his some-time mentor Robinson - have such a strong Christian message now. The Christian right in America can be a good source of funds.Christianity is now a big part of Danny Thomas's brand. His calls for action are peppered with the occasional "Amen", pronounced in the American way, with the first syllable said "ay" rather than "ah".He was pictured at St Lawrence church in south London in February and March.The local diocese told BBC News that while it welcomed "people of various political and ideological perspectives", it remained "committed to the inclusion of all people" and the focus of worship would "always be the person of Christ, who is for everyone".Thomas has spoken publicly about his new-found faith: "I have repented my sins and, under Jesus Christ, I am a new man."Thomas is trying to raise money for Patriot Platform through a popular American Christian crowdfunding platform. Just below the "Give" and "Share" buttons, there is a "Pray" button.On the page, Thomas says he is trying to raise £5,000 a month to pay for the likes of transport, boats and a studio. This month alone he has raised around £9,000. This attempt to build Christianity into the brand is potentially also a way of painting the UK as a Christian country, and Muslim immigrants as outsiders.As for what comes next for the Patriot Platform after its initial surge in supporters, far-right expert Allchorn thinks it's an unclear picture."A lot of these groups don't really have an end goal in mind," he says. "This often comes kind of later on when they are kind of forced to to come up with more concrete proposals and goals."

schema.headline: Anti-migrant activists like Danny Tommo are changing tactics

title: 70 Up: Curtain falls on documentary that has captivated Brits for six decades
description: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing outImage source, ITVImage caption, 70 Up stars from left to right: Peter
body: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing outImage source, ITVImage caption, 70 Up stars from left to right: Peter Davies, Symon Basterfield, Paul Kligerman, Tony Walker Neil Hughes, John Brisby, Andrew Brackfield, Bruce Balden Jackie Bassett, Suzy Lusk, Sue DavisByGeorge WrightSix decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister.It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up.The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age."They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood.Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years.Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday.Image source, ITVImage source, ITV"We didn't really know what we were doing, we had no idea what was happening," Jackie said of the day the Granada TV crew turned up at her school.In the first episode, Jackie appeared alongside her friends, Lynn and Sue, as they were asked questions about boys at school and their hopes for the future. Jackie said she would like to marry a boy "that's not got a lot of money, but has got some money".The nation was also introduced to the likes of wide-eyed Neil, who explained his plans to become either an astronaut or a coach driver; anxious Paul, who ruminated on the idea of one day marrying a woman who made him eat his greens; and pensive Bruce, who said his "heart's desire is to see my daddy who is 6,000 miles away" in Rhodesia.Image source, ITVImage caption, In 7 Up, friends Jackie Bassett, Lynn Johnson and Sue Davis were asked questions about boys and their hopes for the futureImage source, ITVImage caption, 7 Up was intended to be a one-off snapshot of the class system in BritainThe first episode was directed by Canadian Paul Almond, with the help of a young researcher named Michael Apted, who was involved in selecting the children.Apted then decided to follow up on the children seven years later."The material was dreadful – as teenagers, they wouldn't say anything," he later said of the second episode, 7 Plus Seven."Yet we started to realise the power of the idea; despite the film not being very good, everyone was interested in it."Apted went on to become a big name in Hollywood, directing blockbusters including James Bond's The World Is Not Enough, but he always returned to the show and said it was his most significant achievement.Every seven years, millions would tune in for updates on the cast's lives. Neil's dreamy outlook on the world as a child descended into battles with depression, isolation and homelessness, only to turn up as a Liberal Democrat councillor at 42 and then a lay preacher seven years later.Jackie initially said she did not want children, but by 42 Up was an adoring mother to three boys.Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Neil Hughes had battles with depression and homelessness but went on to be a Liberal Democrat councillor and a lay preacherAs the series grew in popularity, Apted started receiving push-back from some of the participants, who felt they had been typecast based on their backgrounds.At 21, Apted asked Jackie - who had recently got married - whether she had met "enough men" before she decided to marry. For the rest of the interview, she mostly looked to the floor while Sue and Lynn answered questions.It took her 28 years to fully confront Apted over his questioning.In 49 Up, she told him: "I was really angry… you wouldn't have asked some of the other people in this programme that question. You will edit this programme as you see fit, I've got no control over that."Recalling the tense exchange, Jackie said she felt Apted could be out of touch, particularly over the changing roles of women in society."I think he still thought we were all in the kitchen, as I mentioned to him at 21. I just thought, 'No, come on, it's about time one of us called you out on it, because he never never asked us questions about politics. It was nearly always domestic," she said.Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Jackie, Lynn and Sue filming 28 Up... Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, ... and filming 35 Up with director Michael Apted on the left Jackie was not the only cast member to clash with Apted.John Brisby, who became a leading barrister, declared in 35 Up that the show felt like a "little pill of poison" injected into his veins every seven years and he wished his headmaster had never put him up for the show. He appeared in later series but refused to be interviewed by Apted.And Charles Furneaux, who later worked at the BBC before becoming commissioning editor at Channel 4, refused to appear after 21 Up following an off-camera argument in which Apted later admitted he went "berserk".Apted acknowledged flaws with the show, saying it was a "horrible error" to have only four women in a cast of 14 when making the original selection.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Michael Apted became a Hollywood director, but always returned to the showFive years ago, Apted passed away, aged 79.The effect he had on the cast is clear in the final episode.Despite their differences, Jackie maintains deep affection and respect for the man she said "opened up a world to me that I would never have known"."I've always said it's a bit like having an uncle in the family. Sometimes you love him and cuddle him to death, and other times you think: I wish he'd just go away."He would always, always help anybody and anything."Nick Hitchon died from cancer in 2023, becoming the second member of the cast to pass away after Lynn Johnson 10 years earlier.Nick, who was born on a farm in the Yorkshire Dales and famously said he wanted to "find out about the moon and all that" in 7 Up, went on to become a scientist and professor at the University of Wisconsin.In his obituary, his brother Andrew wrote Nick "was an expert in nuclear fusion who eventually accepted that he would always be best known for appearing in a ground-breaking TV documentary rather than as a scientist".Image source, ITVImage caption, Nick Hitchon, who went on to become a scientist, passed away in 2023After Apted's death, it was unclear whether 70 Up would happen.But it was announced earlier this year that Asif Kapadia, best known for his documentaries on Amy Winehouse and Diego Maradona, would direct the final chapter.Jackie said she felt apprehensive about having anyone other than Apted in charge, but said Kapadia made her feel immediately at ease. She even welcomed a new approach, saying his interviews felt more like a conversation, while Apted would often leave long, awkward pauses once she had finished her answer.In the final episode, Jackie appears the most content she has been since the age of seven. She attributes this newfound peace to recently moving to Norfolk, from Scotland, where she had been since her thirties. She loves being a mother and grandmother, but said she "needed time for me"."I have that peace around me," she said.Image source, ITVImage caption, Jackie says it is the right time to draw the show to a closeAnd does this episode really mark the end?"I'm not sure any of us will have the energy for it, to be honest," Jackie said. "I think this is the right time to stop, I really do. "Seventy has got a symmetry to it," she said. "We started at seven, we finished at 70 - and that's it."Despite all the plaudits, Jackie has always been slightly perplexed as to why the show has made such an impact, but understands how watching their journeys has helped some people make sense of their own.The series started out being about class but "then they suddenly thought, hang on a minute, this is about life", she said."There's somebody on that programme that just about everybody can associate with. And I think that is something that will outlast all of us."

schema.headline: 70 Up: Curtain falls on documentary that has captivated Brits for six decades
